catalog_quote: Phonological words consist of from one to eight syllables. Their nuclei bear one primary stress. The location of the nuclei in phonological words with one or more long syllables ... is determined by the following rule: Stress occurs on the last long syllable unless that syllable is final in the phonological word. In these cases stress occurs on the second-to-last long syllable ... 2. Stress. Although true minimal pairs for stress in Guahibo have not been found, neither is there any simple way of predicting stress. sweep_summary: Three bibliography items, all by Riena Kondo and all about Sikuani/Guahibo word stress. (1) Kondo 1985 English 'Guahibo: Long vowels and stress' is the catalog's deciding source; it was already held by the project (Rosetta scan) and was re-read — it confirms the weight-hedged coding (stress on the last long syllable unless final, else the second-to-last long syllable; all-light words penult/initial by syllable count; never final; suffix shifts; author hedges predictability). A second copy (SIL archive file, no text layer) was downloaded via the Internet Archive. (2) Kondo 1985 Spanish 'Contribución al estudio de la longitud vocálica y el acento' (ALCA 13: 55-81) was NEW to the per-language bibliography: found through Internet Archive copy of the SIL archive listing (entry 18954), the PDF downloaded from the Internet Archive (live sil.org files are an automated-access block-403), scanned (27 pp, tesseract spa+eng 300 dpi) and read. It is the Spanish translation of the English article (title page credits Larson, Kondo and González) and states the same rules verbatim, with additions: syllable-timed rhythm (2.1), 3-syllable words with only a final long syllable are penultimate and 4-syllable ones antepenultimate (2.2.2), and a phrase-level accent shift when calling from a distance (2.4) — refines, does not supersede. (3) Kondo 2001 IJAL 67(2) 'Guahibo stress: both trochaic and iambic' remains unread: DOI 10.1086/466453 is closed (Unpaywall, Semantic Scholar, Crossref: no OA copy, no abstract), the SIL archive record (entry 2458) holds metadata only and points to JSTOR stable 1265887 (free-account reading), and UChicago/JSTOR pages block fetchers. It is the highest-priority acquisition: per the on-disk Wikipedia paraphrase it reanalyses the light-syllable residue as left-to-right binary feet, lexically trochaic or iambic per morpheme, heavy syllables always stressed, primary stress on the rightmost non-final foot — which, if read first-hand, could move the catalog's kind from weight-hedged to a lexically contrastive foot-based system. Bing/DDG/Mojeek returned junk or 403, so discovery went through SIL archive pages, the Internet Archive's index and the Crossref/S2/Unpaywall APIs. All downloaded files and are under

new_statements.quote: El acento nunca se da en la última sílaba de una palabra monomorfemática con más de una sílaba; por lo tanto, todas las palabras bisílabas tienen el acento en la penúltima. ... En sustantivos trisílabos en los cuales todas las sílabas son cortas, el acento también cae en la penúltima sílaba. ... En la mayoría de los sustantivos con cuatro sílabas, el acento cae en la sílaba inicial (trasantepenúltima). ... Cuando las vocales largas (o diptongos) se dan en monomorfemas, el acento puede ser predicho, basado en la sílaba larga. El acento cae en la última sílaba larga a no ser que esa sílaba sea la final en la palabra fonológica. En este caso el acento cae en la penúltima sílaba larga.
new_statements.translation: Accent never falls on the last syllable of a monomorphemic word of more than one syllable; therefore all disyllabic words have penultimate accent. ... In trisyllabic nouns in which all syllables are short, the accent also falls on the penultimate syllable. ... In most four-syllable nouns the accent falls on the initial (pre-antepenultimate) syllable. ... When long vowels (or diphthongs) occur in monomorphemes, the accent can be predicted from the long syllable. The accent falls on the last long syllable unless that syllable is final in the phonological word. In that case the accent falls on the second-to-last long syllable.

(Spanish version of Kondo 1985 'Guahibo: Long vowels and stress', with additional sections 2.1 and 2.4.)

new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive, unbounded ('last long syllable, unless final') primary stress with a syllable-count default for all-light words (penult in 2-3 syllables, initial in most 4-syllable words), never final, plus suffix-driven shifts and a hedge that no simple rule predicts it — exactly the classification the catalog already carries as weight-hedged/weight-sensitive (tentative) from the English original. The Spanish text adds that rhythm is syllable-timed (2.1), that 3-syllable words with only a final long syllable are penultimate and 4-syllable ones antepenultimate (2.2.2), and that distance-calling shifts the accent at phrase level (2.4).

new_statements.quote: En guahibo el acento no se escribe, ya que no se han encontrado palabras que se distingan por el mero acento, como pasa con las palabras españolas 'papa' y 'papá'. A pesar de esto, el acento sobresaliente en guahibo no es completamente predecible, y las reglas son muy complicadas. [p.10] ... 1. No se acentúa la última sílaba de una palabra monomorfema (sin afijos) de más de una sílaba. 2. Los sustantivos independientes sin afijos se acentúan según el siguiente cuadro. [a. palabras bisílabas: penúltima; b. palabras trisílabas sin vocales largas o diptongos: penúltima; c. palabras de cuatro sílabas sin vocales largas o diptongos: antepenúltima o transantepenúltima (no es predecible); d. palabras con vocal larga o diptongo: con pocas excepciones, en la vocal larga o diptongo más cerca de la última sílaba; nunca en la última] [nota 6, pp.146-147]
new_statements.translation: In Guahibo the accent is not written, since no words have been found that are distinguished by accent alone, as happens with the Spanish words 'papa' and 'papá'. Despite this, the prominent accent in Guahibo is not completely predictable, and the rules are very complicated. ... 1. The last syllable of a monomorphemic word (without affixes) of more than one syllable is not accented. 2. Independent nouns without affixes are accented according to the following table. [a. disyllables: penult; b. trisyllables without long vowels or diphthongs: penult; c. four-syllable words without long vowels or diphthongs: antepenult or pre-antepenult (not predictable); d. words with a long vowel or diphthong: with few exceptions, on the long vowel or diphthong closest to the last syllable; never on the last]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not contrastive (no minimal pairs by accent alone) and never falls on the final syllable of a polysyllabic monomorpheme. In words with a long vowel or diphthong the stress goes, with few exceptions, to the rightmost non-final long syllable. In all-light words it depends on syllable count: penult in 2- and 3-syllable nouns, antepenult or pre-antepenult (unpredictable) in 4-syllable nouns; unaffixed verbs behave similarly but 3-syllable light verbs may be penult or antepenult; 3-syllable light adverbs split unpredictably between penult and antepenult, 4-syllable ones possibly always antepenult. Affixes shift the stress and intonation can affect it; the author calls the rules very complicated and marks the main accent on every polysyllable in the text to help Spanish speakers.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Note 6.5 p.147: with affixes 'a veces se oyen dos acentos' (sometimes two accents are heard). Note 7 pp.147-148: a long affix can carry its own accent and be a phonological word of its own; in a compound the main accent is always the last one and is the only one. Tomo II p.74: the emotive enclitics -bo, -no, -bë can be lengthened considerably and carry the main accent; -rë is always short and never accented.
new_statements.exceptions: Intimate adjectives aqué 'be cold' and asaé 'be strong' are stressed on the final syllable, 'que es un morfema en sí' (p.52). Long-vowel rule holds 'con pocas excepciones'. Four-syllable light nouns and three-syllable light adverbs/verbs are explicitly unpredictable. Long vowels are not written by Guahibo speakers, so the textbook underlines them optionally (p.9). Dialect differences exist even within one settlement (p.7).
new_statements.identity_note: Kondo & Kondo 1967 describe the speech of Barranco Colorado near Orocué on the Meta River (informants Eutimio Vargas and Manuel Granados, 1963-1966). The 1985 chapter (note 1) and the 1985 pedagogical grammar (p.7, note 4 p.146) describe the dialect spoken near San José de Ocuné (Vichada); the grammar notes dialect differences even within one settlement and that its own stress rule table is for that dialect. All are Guahibo/Sikuani proper, not Cuiba or Guayabero.

new_statements.rule_in_words: In monomorphemic phonological words with a long vowel or diphthong, stress falls on the last long syllable unless it is word-final, then on the second-to-last long syllable. In all-short words placement depends on syllable count: penult in 2- and 3-syllable words, initial in most 4-syllable words; never final. Suffixes perturb stress (short suffixes shift it to the root's penult, or to the root's ultima if that is long).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated in the sections read.
new_statements.exceptions: 8 of 55 four-syllable all-short words have antepenultimate stress (p.49-50); vatsáraca 'chachalaca' and sículitsa 'black-headed parrot' violate the long-syllable rule, possibly onomatopoetic (p.51); at least seven words without the expected suffix shift and three with a shift to a non-long ultima (p.51); the direction suffixes -reca and -rena shift stress to the last root syllable after roots in -ba, -ca, -pa, -va (p.53). Conclusion: stress perturbations 'fairly predictable' but morphophonemic changes with certain suffixes complicate the rules (p.54). Five-syllable words undetermined.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement, diachronic within the same authors' work: Kondo & Kondo 1967 (and its 1972 Spanish version, in the Waterhouse volume) treat stress as phonemic/contrastive with three minimal pairs and give no placement rule, whereas Riena Kondo's 1985 chapter and 1985 pedagogical grammar reanalyze the language with phonemic long vowels, from which stress is predictable (rightmost non-final long syllable; syllable-count default in all-light words; never final), and state that no words are distinguished by accent alone. The 1985 grammar explicitly says the 1984a/1985 article corrects errors in the 1972 article, so the later weight-sensitive analysis supersedes the 1967 one. Within the 1985 works there is a residual hedge, not a conflict: 4-syllable all-light nouns (antepenult or pre-antepenult), 3-syllable light verbs and adverbs (penult or antepenult) are called unpredictable, and the 1985 chapter says 'most' 4-syllable words are initial with 8 of 55 antepenultimate.

audit.recode_to: no reclassification now. After reading Kondo 2001: expect the hedge to be lifted (weight-sensitive (tentative) -> weight-sensitive, CVV heavy, heavy syllables obligatorily stressed) and the primary-stress statement to be recast as rightmost non-final foot with lexically specified trochaic/iambic footing of light syllables; weight class (CVV: long vowel or diphthong, no codas) and word domain should stand.

sources.note: Same placement as the catalog's existing statement (weight-sensitive, rightmost non-final long syllable, penult default in 2-3 syllable light words, never final, suffix-driven shifts, hedged as complicated). Adds: stress is non-contrastive; 4-syllable light nouns are antepenult OR pre-antepenult (the 1985 chapter said 'most' initial); verb and adverb classes; two accents heard in affixed words; emotive enclitics taking the main accent; final-stressed intimate adjectives. sources.quote: 5. Suprasegmental phonemes. Suprasegmental features include phonemic stress. 5.1. Stress. Stress is phonemic, as seen in the following examples: /aké/ 'to be cold', /áke/ 'scorpions'; /tásito/ 'fecal material', /tasíto/ 'my leg bone'; /yáhota/ 'with salt', /yahóta/ 'to carry inside'. High pitch tends to occur on stressed syllables. [p.95] ... A syllable is defined as a unit of potential stress placement. [p.95] ... Vowels tend to be slightly longer on stressed than on unstressed syllables. [p.98]

sources.note: Different type: the 1967 paper posits contrastive lexical stress with minimal pairs, whereas the catalog (from Kondo 1985) has weight-sensitive predictable stress. The disagreement is the author's own superseded analysis: Kondo 1985 (p.45) says the earlier V/CV-only syllable analysis 'caused confusion in the study of long vowels' and reanalyzes long vowels as phonemic with stress predictable from them, and the 1985 pedagogical grammar states no words are distinguished by accent alone and that the 1984a article 'corrige errores al artículo publicado en 1972'. sources.quote: Stress never occurs on the final syllable of a multisyllable monomorpheme and therefore all such two-syllable words have penultimate word stress. [...] On three-syllable words (where all syllables are short) stress is penultimate. [...] On most four-syllable words, stress occurs on the initial syllable. [p.49] ... When long vowels (or diphthongs) occur in a monomorpheme, stress can be predicted, based on the long syllable. Stress occurs on the last long syllable unless that syllable is final in the phonological word. In these cases stress occurs on the second-to-last long syllable. [p.50]
